```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

Sensitivity analysis asks how the solution of a model changes when its
inputs change. For a differential equation \(u' = f(u, p, t)\) with initial
value \(u_0\) and parameters \(p\), the local sensitivities are the
derivatives \(\partial u(t) / \partial p\) and \(\partial u(t) / \partial
u_0\); for a scalar cost \(G(u, p)\) of the solution they combine into the
gradient \(dG/dp\). Gradients drive parameter estimation, optimal control,
experimental design and uncertainty propagation.

modelcompR ports the local sensitivity methods of
[SciMLSensitivity.jl](https://github.com/SciML/SciMLSensitivity.jl). This
article covers

* forward sensitivities (`ODEForwardSensitivityProblem()`),
* continuous adjoints (`adjoint_sensitivities()` with `InterpolatingAdjoint()`,
  `BacksolveAdjoint()`, `QuadratureAdjoint()`, `GaussAdjoint()`, ...),
* gradients of a loss through `solve()` (`solve_gradient()`), including
  events,
* parameter estimation with a gradient,
* DAEs, steady states, nonlinear and optimization solutions,
* stochastic differential equations,
* second order sensitivities,
* shadowing methods for chaotic systems.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(modelcompR))
```

## A model to differentiate

Most examples use the Lotka Volterra predator prey model, written
symbolically. When a problem comes from a `System`, the sensitivity
methods use the symbolic Jacobians \(\partial f / \partial u\) and
\(\partial f / \partial p\) of the compiled model, so every vector
Jacobian product is exact.

```{r}
t <- t_nounits
D <- D_nounits
variables("x(t)", "y(t)")
parameters("r", "k", "m", "e")
eqs <- list(D(x) ~ r * x - k * x * y,
            D(y) ~ -m * y + e * x * y)
lv <- mtkcompile(System(eqs, t, name = "lv"))
prob <- ODEProblem(lv, list(x ~ 1, y ~ 1, r ~ 1.5, k ~ 1, m ~ 3, e ~ 1), c(0, 3))
prob$u0
prob$p
```

The order of the unknowns and parameters is chosen by the compiler, so the
results below are always read by name.

## Forward sensitivities

The forward method differentiates the ODE with respect to the parameters
and integrates the sensitivity matrix \(S = \partial u / \partial p\)
alongside the state:
\[
S' = \frac{\partial f}{\partial u} S + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}, \qquad
S(0) = \frac{\partial u_0}{\partial p}.
\]
The augmented system has \(n (1 + n_p)\) equations, so the cost grows with
the number of parameters. It is the method of choice for few parameters,
or when the sensitivities of the whole trajectory are wanted.
`ODEForwardSensitivityProblem()` mirrors the Julia constructor of the same
name; it accepts an `ODEProblem`, a compiled `System` or a plain R
function.

```{r}
fprob <- ODEForwardSensitivityProblem(prob)
fsol <- solve(fprob, Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
```

`extract_local_sensitivities()` splits the augmented solution into the
state `u` and the sensitivities `du`, one entry per parameter. With an
index it returns one saved time; with `t` it interpolates; with
`asmatrix = TRUE` the sensitivities form one \(n \times n_p\) matrix.

```{r}
last <- extract_local_sensitivities(fsol, length(fsol$t))
last$u
last$du$r
extract_local_sensitivities(fsol, t = 1.5, asmatrix = TRUE)
```

Without an index the function returns the whole trajectory: `u` is a
matrix with one row per saved time, and each element of `du` is a matrix of
the same shape.

```{r}
traj <- extract_local_sensitivities(fsol)
dim(traj$u)
matplot(fsol$t, cbind(traj$du$r, traj$du$m), type = "l", lty = c(1, 1, 2, 2),
        col = c(1, 2, 1, 2), xlab = "t", ylab = "sensitivity")
legend("bottomleft", c("dx/dr", "dy/dr", "dx/dm", "dy/dm"), lty = c(1, 1, 2, 2),
       col = c(1, 2, 1, 2), bty = "n")
```

The sensitivities grow along the oscillation: a small change in the
growth rate shifts the phase of the cycle, and the phase error accumulates.

### Derivatives with respect to the initial values

`ForwardSensitivity()` (the default) differentiates with respect to the
parameters. `ForwardDiffSensitivity()`, Julia's dual number method, can
also differentiate with respect to the initial values; the seed matrices
`du0` and `dp` choose the directions. Each column of the seeds is one
direction \((\delta u_0, \delta p)\). For \(u' = -p u\), \(u(0) = 1\),
\(p = 2\), the derivatives of \(u(1) = e^{-2}\) are \(e^{-2}\) with respect
to \(u_0\) and \(-e^{-2}\) with respect to \(p\):

```{r}
dprob <- ODEForwardSensitivityProblem(function(u, p, t) -p[1] * u, 1, c(0, 1), 2,
                                      sensealg = ForwardDiffSensitivity(),
                                      du0 = cbind(1, 0), dp = cbind(0, 1))
dsol <- solve(dprob, Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-12)
extract_local_sensitivities(dsol, t = 1, asmatrix = TRUE)$du
c(exp(-2), -exp(-2))
```

`ODEForwardSensitivityFunction()` returns the right-hand side of the
augmented system itself, for use with other tools.

```{r}
ODEForwardSensitivityFunction(prob)
```

## Adjoint sensitivities

When there are many parameters and one scalar cost, the adjoint method is
cheaper. For a cost
\[
G(p) = \int_{t_0}^{T} g(u, p, t)\, dt + \sum_i g_i(u(t_i))
\]
it solves the adjoint equation backward in time,
\[
\lambda' = -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial u}\right)^{\!T} \lambda
- \left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial u}\right)^{\!T}, \qquad
\frac{dG}{dp} = \lambda(t_0)^T \frac{\partial u_0}{\partial p}
+ \int_{t_0}^{T} \left(\lambda^T \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}
+ \frac{\partial g}{\partial p}\right) dt,
\]
with jumps \(\lambda \mathrel{+}= \partial g_i / \partial u\) at the
discrete cost times. One backward solve of \(n\) equations (plus a
quadrature of \(n_p\)) gives the whole gradient, whatever the number of
parameters.

`adjoint_sensitivities(sol, alg, ...)` takes a forward solution and
returns `du0` and `dp`. A discrete cost is given by its gradient
`dgdu_discrete(u, p, t, i)` at the times `t`; a continuous cost by `g(u, p,
t)` (its gradients are then taken by finite differences) or by
`dgdu_continuous` and `dgdp_continuous`. The forward solution must be
dense, so it is solved without `saveat`.

```{r}
sol <- solve(prob, Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10)
ts <- seq(0.5, 3, by = 0.5)
# G = sum_i x(t_i): the gradient of the cost at each time is the unit vector of x
ix <- match("x(t)", names(prob$u0))
ex <- replace(numeric(2), ix, 1)
adj <- adjoint_sensitivities(sol, Tsit5(), t = ts, dgdu_discrete = function(u, p, t, i) ex,
                             abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
adj$du0
adj$dp
```

### The adjoint methods

The methods differ in how they obtain the forward state during the
backward solve and how they integrate the parameter gradient:

| Method | Forward state | Parameter gradient |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `InterpolatingAdjoint()` | interpolated from the dense forward solution (or re-solved between checkpoints) | integrated with \(\lambda\) |
| `BacksolveAdjoint()` | integrated backward with \(\lambda\) (reset at the saved points with `checkpointing = TRUE`) | integrated with \(\lambda\) |
| `QuadratureAdjoint()` | interpolated | adaptive Gauss Kronrod quadrature after the backward solve |
| `GaussAdjoint()` | interpolated (or checkpointed) | Gauss Legendre rule on each backward step |
| `GaussKronrodAdjoint()` | interpolated (or checkpointed) | Gauss Kronrod rule on each backward step |

`BacksolveAdjoint()` needs the least memory but can be unstable when the
backward integration of the state is ill conditioned. `GaussAdjoint()` is
the default of `solve_gradient()` for larger problems, as in Julia. All
methods give the same gradient to the solver tolerances:

```{r}
methods <- list(InterpolatingAdjoint = InterpolatingAdjoint(),
                Interpolating_checkpointed = InterpolatingAdjoint(checkpointing = TRUE),
                BacksolveAdjoint = BacksolveAdjoint(),
                QuadratureAdjoint = QuadratureAdjoint(abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10),
                GaussAdjoint = GaussAdjoint(),
                GaussKronrodAdjoint = GaussKronrodAdjoint())
grads <- t(vapply(methods, function(sa) {
  r <- adjoint_sensitivities(sol, Tsit5(), t = ts, dgdu_discrete = function(u, p, t, i) ex,
                             sensealg = sa, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
  c(r$du0, r$dp)
}, numeric(6)))
signif(grads, 8)
```

The forward sensitivities give the same numbers: \(dG/dp = \sum_i
\partial x(t_i) / \partial p\).

```{r}
fs <- extract_local_sensitivities(fsol, t = ts, asmatrix = TRUE)
Reduce(`+`, lapply(fs, function(s) s$du["x(t)", ]))
```

A continuous cost works the same way. Here \(G = \int_0^3 x(t)^2\, dt\):

```{r}
adjoint_sensitivities(sol, Tsit5(), g = function(u, p, t) u[ix]^2,
                      sensealg = GaussAdjoint(), abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)$dp
```

### The adjoint problem

`ODEAdjointProblem()` builds the backward problem without solving it. It
is an ordinary `ODEProblem` with a reversed time span; its `finish`
element turns the backward solution into the gradients.

```{r}
ap <- ODEAdjointProblem(sol, GaussAdjoint(), Tsit5(), t = ts,
                        dgdu_discrete = function(u, p, t, i) ex)
ap$tspan
asol <- solve(ap, Tsit5(), abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
ap$finish(asol)$dp
```

### Vector Jacobian products

In Julia, `autojacvec` selects the automatic differentiation backend that
computes the products \(\lambda^T \partial f / \partial u\) and
\(\lambda^T \partial f / \partial p\): `ZygoteVJP()`, `EnzymeVJP()`,
`ReverseDiffVJP()`, `TrackerVJP()`, `MooncakeVJP()` or `ReactantVJP()`. R
has no automatic differentiation, so in modelcompR

* `autojacvec = NULL` or `TRUE` (and every backend object above) uses the
  symbolic derivatives of the `System`, compiled to R code, or the
  problem's `jac` when it was built from an R function;
* `autojacvec = FALSE` uses central finite differences.

The backend names are accepted so that code translated from Julia runs
unchanged:

```{r}
ZygoteVJP()
sa_list <- list(symbolic = GaussAdjoint(autojacvec = TRUE),
                zygote = GaussAdjoint(autojacvec = ZygoteVJP()),
                enzyme = InterpolatingAdjoint(autojacvec = EnzymeVJP()),
                reversediff = InterpolatingAdjoint(autojacvec = ReverseDiffVJP(compile = TRUE)),
                finite_differences = GaussAdjoint(autojacvec = FALSE))
vapply(sa_list, function(sa) {
  adjoint_sensitivities(sol, Tsit5(), t = ts, dgdu_discrete = function(u, p, t, i) ex,
                        sensealg = sa, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)$dp[["r"]]
}, 0)
```

The discretize then optimize methods `ZygoteAdjoint()`,
`EnzymeAdjoint()`, `ReverseDiffAdjoint()`, `TrackerAdjoint()` and
`MooncakeAdjoint()`, which differentiate through the solver in Julia, run
the forward sensitivities of the discretized solve in R
(`ForwardDiffSensitivity()`), and so give the derivative of the computed
solution.

```{r}
ZygoteAdjoint()
```

## Gradients of a loss through solve

`solve_gradient(loss, prob, alg, ...)` is the R counterpart of calling
`Zygote.gradient` on a function that solves an ODE in Julia. `loss` is any
R function of the solution that returns a number; the options in `...`
go to `solve()` (`saveat`, tolerances, callbacks), and `sensealg` picks
the method. The result holds the gradients `u0` and `p`, the loss `value`
and the forward solution `sol`.

The loss below compares the predator prey trajectory at saved times with
a target. Only the saved values may enter the loss: the adjoint knows the
cotangent of the loss at the `saveat` points.

```{r}
ts <- seq(0, 3, by = 0.25)
loss <- function(sol) sum((sol[x] - 1)^2) + sum(sol[y])
g_fwd <- solve_gradient(loss, prob, Tsit5(), saveat = ts, reltol = 1e-9, abstol = 1e-10,
                        sensealg = ForwardDiffSensitivity())
g_adj <- solve_gradient(loss, prob, Tsit5(), saveat = ts, reltol = 1e-9, abstol = 1e-10,
                        sensealg = GaussAdjoint())
g_fwd$value
rbind(forward = c(g_fwd$u0, g_fwd$p), adjoint = c(g_adj$u0, g_adj$p))
```

A central finite difference check:

```{r}
F <- function(th) loss(solve(remake(prob, u0 = th[1:2], p = th[3:6]), Tsit5(),
                             reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10, saveat = ts))
th <- c(prob$u0, prob$p)
fd <- vapply(seq_along(th), function(j) {
  h <- replace(numeric(6), j, 1e-5)
  (F(th + h) - F(th - h)) / 2e-5
}, 0)
max(abs(fd - c(g_adj$u0, g_adj$p)))
```

When `sensealg` is not given, `solve_gradient()` picks one from the
problem: forward sensitivities for small ODEs, `GaussAdjoint()` for larger
ones, `SteadyStateAdjoint()` for nonlinear and steady state problems.

### Events

Events are differentiated too, including the dependence of the event time
on the parameters. A ball dropped from height \(x_0\) bounces at
\(x = 0\) with restitution \(e\); the loss is the height at \(t = 0.8\),
after the bounce.

```{r}
variables("h(t)", "v(t)")
parameters("grav", "rest")
ball <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(h) ~ v, D(v) ~ -grav), t, name = "ball",
                          continuous_events = list(list(h ~ 0), list(v ~ -rest * Pre(v)))))
bprob <- ODEProblem(ball, list(h ~ 1, v ~ 0, grav ~ 9.81, rest ~ 0.9), c(0, 0.8))
height <- function(sol) tail(sol[h], 1)
gb <- solve_gradient(height, bprob, Tsit5(), saveat = 0.8, reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-12,
                     sensealg = InterpolatingAdjoint())
gb$value
gb$p
```

The exact height after the bounce is
\(-e\, v_\tau (T - \tau) - g (T - \tau)^2 / 2\) with \(\tau =
\sqrt{2 x_0 / g}\) and \(v_\tau = -g \tau\), so
\(\partial x(T) / \partial e = g \tau (T - \tau)\):

```{r}
tau <- sqrt(2 / 9.81)
9.81 * tau * (0.8 - tau)
```

To use `adjoint_sensitivities()` directly on a problem with events, solve
it with `solve(prob, alg, sensealg = ...)`, which records the events for
the backward pass.

## Parameter estimation with a gradient

A gradient makes local optimizers converge in a few iterations. The
logistic growth model \(N' = \rho N (1 - N / K)\) is fitted to noisy
observations with `stats::optim()` and the bounded quasi Newton method L-BFGS-B; `solve_gradient()`
supplies both the loss and its gradient. The parameters are optimized on
the log scale to keep them positive.

```{r}
variables("N(t)")
parameters("rho", "K")
logistic <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(N) ~ rho * N * (1 - N / K)), t, name = "logistic"))
lprob <- ODEProblem(logistic, list(N ~ 0.1, rho ~ 1.2, K ~ 2), c(0, 8))
tobs <- seq(0, 8, by = 0.5)
set.seed(1)
truth <- solve(lprob, Tsit5(), saveat = tobs, reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10)[N]
Nobs <- truth + rnorm(length(tobs), sd = 0.05)

pnames <- names(lprob$p)
sse <- function(sol) sum((sol[N] - Nobs)^2)
cache <- new.env()
objective <- function(logp) {
  if (!identical(cache$logp, logp)) {   # optim asks for fn and gr at the same point
    pr <- remake(lprob, p = setNames(exp(logp), pnames))
    cache$res <- solve_gradient(sse, pr, Tsit5(), saveat = tobs, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-10)
    cache$logp <- logp
  }
  cache$res
}
fn <- function(logp) objective(logp)$value
gr <- function(logp) objective(logp)$p * exp(logp)   # chain rule for log parameters

start <- log(c(rho = 0.5, K = 1))[pnames]
fit <- optim(start, fn, gr, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = log(0.05), upper = log(20))
exp(fit$par)
fit$counts
```

The bounds keep the line search away from growth rates so large that the
ODE becomes extremely stiff; an unbounded BFGS search on the log scale can
try \(\rho = e^{30}\) in its first step.

The estimates are close to the true values \(\rho = 1.2\) and \(K = 2\).

```{r}
fitted <- solve(remake(lprob, p = setNames(exp(fit$par), pnames)), Tsit5())
plot(tobs, Nobs, xlab = "t", ylab = "N", pch = 19)
tt <- seq(0, 8, length.out = 200)
lines(tt, vapply(tt, function(s) fitted(s)[[1]], 0), col = 2)
```

## Differential algebraic equations

Semi-explicit DAEs compiled from a `System` become mass matrix ODEs with
zero rows for the algebraic equations. The interpolating, quadrature and
Gauss adjoints handle them, as do the forward methods; the algebraic
initial values are recomputed from the constraint, so their gradient is
zero.

```{r}
variables("w(t)", "z(t)")
parameters("kd", "ad")
dsys <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(w) ~ -kd * z, 0 ~ z^3 + z - ad * w), t, name = "dae"))
daeprob <- ODEProblem(dsys, list(w ~ 1, kd ~ 0.7, ad ~ 0.5), c(0, 2), jac = TRUE,
                      guesses = list(z ~ 0.5))
dloss <- function(sol) sum(sol[w]^2) + 3 * sum(sol[z])
dts <- seq(0, 2, by = 0.5)
gd <- solve_gradient(dloss, daeprob, Rodas5P(), saveat = dts, reltol = 1e-9, abstol = 1e-10,
                     sensealg = GaussAdjoint())
gd$u0
gd$p
```

Fully implicit DAEs \(F(u', u, p, t) = 0\) (a `DAEProblem`) have their own
adjoint, `DAEAdjointProblem()`, used by `adjoint_sensitivities()`. The
residual below couples \(u_1' = -p_1 u_1 + u_2\) with the algebraic equation
\(u_2 = p_2 u_1\), so \(u_1' = -(p_1 - p_2) u_1\). With \(u_1(0) = 1\),
\(p = (1, 0.5)\), the cost \(G = u_1(1) = e^{-(p_1 - p_2)}\) has gradient
\((-1, 1)\, e^{-0.5}\) in \(p\):

```{r}
res <- function(du, u, p, t) c(du[1] + p[1] * u[1] - u[2], u[2] - p[2] * u[1])
iprob <- DAEProblem(res, c(-0.5, 0), c(1, 0.5), c(0, 1), c(1, 0.5),
                    differential_vars = c(TRUE, FALSE))
isol <- solve(iprob, DFBDF(), abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
ir <- adjoint_sensitivities(isol, DFBDF(), t = 1, dgdu_discrete = function(u, p, t, i) c(1, 0),
                            abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
ir$dp
c(-1, 1) * exp(-0.5)
```

## Steady states and nonlinear solutions

For a steady state \(f(u^*, p) = 0\), the implicit function theorem gives
\(\partial u^* / \partial p = -(\partial f / \partial u)^{-1} \partial f /
\partial p\) without differentiating the iterations of the solver. The
adjoint form needs one linear solve with the transposed Jacobian;
`SteadyStateAdjoint()` implements it.

The steady state of \(x' = s - k x^2\) is \(x^* = \sqrt{s / k}\), so
\(G = x^{*2} = s / k\) has \(\partial G / \partial k = -s / k^2 = -3/4\) and
\(\partial G / \partial s = 1 / k = 1/2\) at \(k = 2\), \(s = 3\).

```{r}
variables("q(t)")
parameters("kq", "sq")
ss <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(q) ~ sq - kq * q^2), t, name = "ss"))
ssprob <- SteadyStateProblem(ss, list(q ~ 1, kq ~ 2, sq ~ 3))
sssol <- solve(ssprob, SSRootfind())
adjoint_sensitivities(sssol, NULL, sensealg = SteadyStateAdjoint(), g = function(u, p) u[1]^2)$dp
solve_gradient(function(sol) sol$u[[1]]^2, ssprob, SSRootfind())$p
```

Nonlinear problems work the same way. For the system \(u_1^2 = p_1\),
\(u_2 = p_2 u_1\), the loss \(u_1 + u_2\) has gradient
\((1 + p_2) / (2 \sqrt{p_1})\) in \(p_1\) and \(\sqrt{p_1}\) in \(p_2\):

```{r}
nprob <- NonlinearProblem(function(u, p) c(u[1]^2 - p[1], u[2] - p[2] * u[1]), c(1, 1),
                          p = c(2, 3))
solve_gradient(function(sol) sum(sol$u), nprob, NewtonRaphson())$p
c(4 / (2 * sqrt(2)), sqrt(2))
```

The optimum of an `OptimizationProblem` is differentiated through its
optimality conditions: `UnconstrainedOptimizationAdjoint()` without
constraints, `OptimizationAdjoint()` (the KKT conditions) with them. The
minimizer of \((x_1 - p_1)^2 + (x_2 - p_2 x_1)^2\) is \(x_1 = p_1\),
\(x_2 = p_1 p_2\), so the loss \(x_1 + x_2\) has gradient \((1 + p_2, p_1)\):

```{r}
fq <- function(x, p) (x[1] - p[1])^2 + (x[2] - p[2] * x[1])^2
oprob <- OptimizationProblem(fq, c(0, 0), c(1, 3))
solve_gradient(function(sol) sum(sol$u), oprob, BFGS(), g_abstol = 1e-12)$p
```

## Stochastic differential equations

For an SDE, `solve_gradient()` with a fixed step method, a `dt` and a
`seed` differentiates the sampled path: the noise is held fixed and the
result is the pathwise derivative. For geometric Brownian motion
\(du = \mu u\, dt + \sigma u\, dW\) the path is
\(u(T) = u_0 \exp((\mu - \sigma^2 / 2) T + \sigma W_T)\), so
\(\partial u(T) / \partial \mu = T u(T)\).

```{r}
sprob <- SDEProblem(function(u, p, t) p[1] * u, function(u, p, t) p[2] * u, 1, c(0, 1),
                    c(1.5, 0.3))
send <- function(sol) tail(as.matrix(sol)[, 1], 1)
gs <- solve_gradient(send, sprob, EM(), dt = 0.01, seed = 3)
c(du0 = gs$u0, dp = gs$p)
gs$value   # u(T), and T u(T) since T = 1
```

The derivative in \(u_0\) equals \(u(T) / u_0\) exactly, since the path is
linear in \(u_0\). The derivative in \(\mu\) is close to, but not equal to,
\(T u(T)\): the pathwise derivative is that of the discrete Euler Maruyama
path \(u_N = u_0 \prod_k (1 + \mu\, \Delta t + \sigma\, \Delta W_k)\), which is
\(u_N \sum_k \Delta t / (1 + \mu\, \Delta t + \sigma\, \Delta W_k)\).

The adjoint methods `BacksolveAdjoint()` and `InterpolatingAdjoint()`
also run on SDEs (`SDEAdjointProblem()`) and random ODEs
(`RODEAdjointProblem()`). They need the noise path to be reproducible
backward in time, which a `NoiseGrid` provides:

```{r}
tg <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.05)
W <- 0.3 * sin(3.1 * tg) + 0.25 * sin(7.3 * tg)
nprob2 <- SDEProblem(function(u, p, t) c(p[1] * u[1] - u[1] * u[2], -p[2] * u[2] + u[1] * u[2]),
                     function(u, p, t) c(p[3] * u[1], p[3] * u[2]),
                     c(1, 0.8), c(0, 1), c(1.2, 0.9, 0.3),
                     noise = NoiseGrid(tg, cbind(W, -W)))
ssol <- solve(nprob2, EulerHeun(), dt = 0.05)
for (sa in list(BacksolveAdjoint(), InterpolatingAdjoint()))
  print(adjoint_sensitivities(ssol, EulerHeun(), t = c(0.5, 1),
                              dgdu_discrete = function(u, p, t, i) u, sensealg = sa)$dp)
```

With a Stratonovich method such as `EulerHeun()` the adjoint is solved with
the same scheme; with an Ito method the drift is corrected first (see
`StochasticTransformedFunction()`). With `noisemixing = TRUE` the full
Jacobian of a diagonal noise term enters the adjoint.

## Second order sensitivities

`second_order_sensitivities(loss, prob, alg, ...)` returns the Hessian of
a loss with respect to the parameters, and
`second_order_sensitivity_product(loss, v, prob, alg, ...)` the product of
the Hessian with a vector \(v\), the building block of Newton Krylov
methods. Julia's `ForwardDiffOverAdjoint()` runs forward mode automatic
differentiation over an adjoint gradient; modelcompR takes central
differences of the adjoint gradient of `solve_gradient()`, so the solves
should use tight tolerances.

For \(u' = -p_1 p_2 u\), \(u(0) = 1\), the loss \(u(1) = e^{-p_1 p_2}\) has
the Hessian
\[
e^{-p_1 p_2} \begin{pmatrix} p_2^2 & p_1 p_2 - 1 \\ p_1 p_2 - 1 & p_1^2 \end{pmatrix},
\]
which at \(p = (2, 0.5)\) is \(e^{-1} \operatorname{diag}(0.25, 4)\).

```{r}
eprob <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) -p[1] * p[2] * u, 1, c(0, 1), c(2, 0.5))
eloss <- function(sol) sol$u[[length(sol$t)]]
H <- second_order_sensitivities(eloss, eprob, Tsit5(), saveat = 1, reltol = 1e-12,
                                abstol = 1e-12)
round(H, 6)
exp(-1) * diag(c(0.25, 4))
second_order_sensitivity_product(eloss, c(1, 1), eprob, Tsit5(), saveat = 1,
                                 reltol = 1e-12, abstol = 1e-12)
```

## Shadowing methods for chaotic systems

In a chaotic system nearby trajectories separate exponentially, so the
ordinary sensitivities of a long time average grow without bound and are
useless. The average itself, for example the mean height \(\langle z
\rangle\) of the Lorenz attractor, still depends smoothly on the
parameters. Shadowing methods compute that derivative by finding a
perturbed trajectory that stays close to the original one.

* `ForwardLSS()` and `AdjointLSS()` (least squares shadowing) solve one
  large least squares problem on the saved points of a solution; the
  regularizer `TimeDilation()`, `CosWindowing()` or `Cos2Windowing()`
  chooses how the time average is handled.
* `NILSS()` and `NILSAS()` (non intrusive LSS and its adjoint) work in the
  unstable subspace only, integrating a few tangent or adjoint solutions
  over `nseg` segments of `nstep` saved points.

The derivative of \(\langle z \rangle\) with respect to \(\rho\) is close
to 1 (Lea, Allen and Haine, 2000).

```{r}
lorenz <- function(u, p, t) c(p[1] * (u[2] - u[1]), u[1] * (p[2] - u[3]) - u[2],
                              u[1] * u[2] - p[3] * u[3])
u_attr <- c(-12.808828477348253, -18.197181420445414, 25.88373061170027)
lprob3 <- ODEProblem(lorenz, u_attr, c(0, 10), c(10, 28, 8 / 3))
gz <- function(u, p, t) u[3]
lsol <- solve(lprob3, Tsit5(), saveat = 0.02, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
lss_f <- shadow_forward(ForwardLSSProblem(lsol, ForwardLSS(g = gz)))
lss_a <- shadow_adjoint(AdjointLSSProblem(lsol, AdjointLSS(g = gz)))
rbind(ForwardLSS = lss_f, AdjointLSS = lss_a)
```

The second entry, the derivative in \(\rho\), is close to 1. NILSS integrates
the tangent equations on short segments from the initial point:

```{r}
nilss <- shadow_forward(NILSSProblem(lprob3, NILSS(10, 51, g = gz, seed = 1)), Tsit5(),
                        reltol = 1e-6, abstol = 1e-6)
nilss
```

`NILSASProblem(sol, NILSAS(nseg, nstep, M, g = g), alg)` is the adjoint
counterpart; it takes a dense solution and `M` homogeneous adjoint
solutions (at least the number of positive Lyapunov exponents plus one).

## Summary

| Task | modelcompR | Julia |
|:--|:--|:--|
| forward sensitivities | `ODEForwardSensitivityProblem()`, `extract_local_sensitivities()` | the same |
| adjoint of a cost | `adjoint_sensitivities()`, `ODEAdjointProblem()` | the same |
| gradient of a loss of `solve()` | `solve_gradient(loss, prob, alg, ...)` | `Zygote.gradient` of a function calling `solve` |
| DAE, SDE, RODE adjoints | `DAEAdjointProblem()`, `SDEAdjointProblem()`, `RODEAdjointProblem()` | the same |
| steady states, nonlinear and optimization solutions | `SteadyStateAdjoint()`, `OptimizationAdjoint()` | the same |
| Hessians | `second_order_sensitivities()`, `second_order_sensitivity_product()` | the same |
| chaotic averages | `ForwardLSS()`, `AdjointLSS()`, `NILSS()`, `NILSAS()` with `shadow_forward()`, `shadow_adjoint()` | `shadow_forward`, `shadow_adjoint` |
